This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button. How the All Blacks rated in their 33-16 win over South Africa at Ellis Park. Busy around the field despite being hampered by a knee injury but must be judged by the performance of the scrum which was poor in the first half. The
All Blacks had six feeds, were penalised twice, and were going backwards on two. De Groot was penalised at one scrum which led to three points. Was also pinged at the breakdown. Six carries in first half. Off after 37 minutes with a head knock. A real mixed bag. Lost an early turnover and was penalised before being marched 10m for keeping the ball away from the Bok halfback. Also caused a penalty advantage before the Boks scored a try. The scrum was a mess but the lineout was solid when Taylor was throwing. Strong around the field with five carries and finished with the side’s second most tackles completed with 12. All Blacks were done at the scrum in the first half and the front rowers have to wear that. Was also penalised for not releasing with Boks inside own half. Finished with eight tackles in 50 minutes of game time. A shame to leave the field after a head clash with de Groot as he was starting to get into the test. Gave away an early penalty for taking out a man at lineout. But forced a knock-on with a tackle on Ox Nche. Won three lineouts. Off after 37 minutes. The brilliant charge-down try changed the test coming off a South African penalty to take a 16-12 lead. Suddenly, thanks to Holland, the All Blacks took the lead themselves and didn’t look back. He was later penalised for a neck roll penalty with his team on attack. Put in constant pressure at the lineout and won a turnover from a tackle. Strong defensive effort. Superb test playing the first half at loose forward then switching to lock when Lord left. Played wide on attack early on, giving Kurt-Lee Arendse trouble early before finding space on the left to set up Josh Moorby’s try with a great ball. Looks like the No 7 jersey is locked up for the moment. Jacobson had some good charging runs early on but was clutching air in an attempt on Cheslin Kolbe (there’s a long list of defenders in that club). Scored from short distance and had to beat the attempted tackle from Pieter-Steph du Toit to do so (not many attackers in that club). Last played against Ireland a month ago and showed no sign of rust at Ellis Park. Good strong runs early. Held up a try and set up both Jacobson and Jordan from the back of the scrum runs, a classy wide assist for Jordan’s second. Finished with 11 tackles and eight carries in a strong all-round effort, though he wasn’t a major threat at the breakdown. A massive force off the scrum when it’s going forward. Another player who went into the test short of recent game time and probably didn’t reach his usual high standard. Mixed efforts from box kicks but did have one great clearance under pressure on own line. A bullet pass to Jordan for opening try. Didn’t leave a massive impression on the test. Good early kicks for touch, and landed four from five off the tee. Was beaten in the air but made a try-saving tackle. Took a heavy hit to his shoulder stopping Eben Etzebeth which looked to be the end of his night – but played on. Missed a one-on-one tackle on Andre Esterhuizen which led to the Springboks try. But made up for that with a good finish, beating the tackle of du Toit to score the All Blacks’ second try. Just four carries. Off after 63 minutes. A defensive work-horse right until the late minute of the test. Came up with two key defensive plays first denying Malcolm Marx over the tryline with a strip and then again ripped the ball from a charging Jasper Wiese inside 10m just before halftime. Did it again to Wiese in the closing stages. Finished with 15 tackles, the most of the test, and won five turnovers, the most of the test. Even managed to join a rolling maul. While Jordan got the plaudits, Barrett was the real man of the match. Lost the contest in the air a few times against Damian Willemse and didn’t have a massive test on the defensive end. However, two smart plays kept the All Blacks in control – taking a kickoff inside the in-goal to win a scrum at halfway and a crucial 50-22 in the final quarter. Scored two relatively easy tries, but Jordan finished with seven defenders beaten and he also put McKenzie into a break that almost saw a try. Got away with a few mistakes – took a quick tap inside the 22 only to have his kick charged down, batted a high ball back too far which left Love chasing and led to a South African lineout on attack, and he dropped one ball cold. Won a key turnover but also responsible for five turnovers lost. Coming off injury watch and fairly ineffective in the first half, but made his mark in the second 40. A great line break midway through the second half almost led to a try. Started to find his way once South Africa started chasing and moved away from box kicks. Finished with two turnovers. Scrum certainly improved when he entered the game, but lost two lineouts. Made eight tackles. Huge impact from the bench to stop the scrum going backwards. Should have earned himself a starting spot for the second test, joining Bower in at least ensuring the scrum was a level contest. Late call-up for Anton Segner and entered the game early after Lord went off in the 37th minute. Finished with eight tackles. Little time to make an impact but looked busy in the five minutes he was on the field. Only on for the last five to experience the Ellis Park atmosphere. On for the last 17 minutes and didn’t get a carry. Cameron McMillan has been a sports journalist since 2003 and is NZME’s Deputy Head of Sport. title: The Hyundai Ioniq V Is Everything We Want From An EV... But Can't Have - Yahoo Autos
content: Hyundai has built the sort of affordable electric car Western buyers keep asking automakers to make. It looks dramatic, has the footprint of a midsize sedan, offers genuinely useful range, and starts at the equivalent of less than $18,000. There is one rather important catch, however. The new Ioniq V is launching in China, and Hyundai has not announced plans to sell it in the United States or Europe, leaving everyone outside its home market to admire the specification sheet from afar. That is particularly frustrating because this is no tiny bargain-bin commuter built solely around a low sticker price. The Ioniq V looks like something Lamborghini designed, stretches almost 193 inches long, packs a massive 27-inch display inside, and offers up to 225 horsepower with a claimed 404 miles of range. CarNewsChina reports that pre-sales have now opened at 119,900 yuan, equivalent to roughly $17,800 at the time of writing. For perspective, that makes this Camry-sized electric sedan cheaper than the least expensive new car currently offered in the United States. The Ioniq V was developed specifically for China through Beijing Hyundai, and its design makes it difficult to mistake for one of the brand's conservative fleet sedans. Its low nose, sharply sculpted body, frameless doors, fastback roofline, and angular lighting give it an almost concept-car appearance. There are even hints of Lamborghini-style wedge design in its proportions, although the overall execution remains distinctly Hyundai. Buyers can also escape the usual sea of gray, black, and silver with colors including Cyber Gold, Gamma Green, and Dimensional Purple. Size is another surprise, as the Ioniq V measures 4,900 mm, or 192.9 inches, from nose to tail and rides on a 2,900-mm, or 114.2-inch, wheelbase. That puts it squarely into familiar midsize-sedan territory. A current Hyundai Sonata is roughly 193.3 inches long, while a Toyota Camry measures about 193.5 inches. Things get equally ambitious once you open the door. Dominating the dashboard is a 27-inch display backed by Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8295 processor, supplemented by a head-up display Hyundai calls Cyber Eye. The infotainment system incorporates artificial-intelligence technology from Chinese companies Baidu and ByteDance. Driver-assistance technology comes from Momenta, while Hyundai also lists nine airbags and an extensive collection of active safety systems. That combination shows how fiercely competitive China's EV market has become. A low price alone is no longer enough when domestic brands regularly offer enormous screens, advanced software, sophisticated driver assistance, and surprisingly premium interiors at mainstream prices. Three versions are initially available. The Standard Edition starts at 119,900 yuan, or around $17,800, while the Smart Driving Edition rises to roughly $19,300 and the Long Range version costs approximately $20,800. Power comes from a single electric motor driving the rear wheels, producing either 188 horsepower or 225 horsepower depending on configuration. CATL supplies lithium-iron-phosphate battery packs with capacities of 53.5 kWh and 66.8 kWh. Claimed range stretches from approximately 323 miles to 404 miles, depending on specification. Those figures use China's CLTC testing procedure, which is considerably more optimistic than the EPA cycle, so the American-rated range would be noticeably lower. Even allowing for that difference, the numbers remain impressive considering the price. The larger-battery version costs barely $3,000 more than the entry model while delivering substantially greater range and additional power. The Ioniq V uses Hyundai's E-GMP architecture and an 800-volt electrical system, but Hyundai has not yet disclosed its maximum charging rate, although the company's existing 800-volt EVs have established a strong reputation for rapid DC charging. The Ioniq V illustrates an increasingly uncomfortable reality for buyers watching China's EV market from elsewhere. Chinese consumers now have access to large, technologically sophisticated electric cars at prices that would barely buy an entry-level gasoline-powered vehicle in the United States. Hyundai clearly needs aggressive pricing to compete there. China's EV sector includes a huge collection of domestic manufacturers fighting over customers, forcing established international companies to deliver better specifications for less money. Hyundai has indicated that lessons learned from its Chinese EV program could eventually influence vehicles sold globally, and the company reportedly intends to expand the design philosophy across a much larger local lineup. That still doesn't give Western buyers a date for the Ioniq V itself. Perhaps it will eventually reach markets such as Australia, Europe, or Canada. For now, though, the Ioniq V is exactly the kind of affordable, stylish electric sedan many buyers say they want — unfortunately, it's parked on the wrong side of the world. title: Springboks 16-33 All Blacks: 5 takeaways as 'brutal scrum obliteration' matters little - Planet Rugby
content: Tupou Vaa'i in action for All Blacks against Springboks. Following an epic start to Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry Test series, here are our five takeaways from the All Blacks’ 33-16 victory over the Springboks at Ellis Park in Johannesburg. Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry Test series certainly got the greatest introduction, as not only did South Africa and New Zealand go hammer and tongs at one another, but Johannesburg put on a belter of a show before the first whistle. The highveld has been bitterly cold over the past few weeks, but the sun appeared on Friday and stayed until today, providing the perfect conditions for the two great rivals to collide. Despite the eye-watering price tags, Ellis Park was PACKED. Fans arrived in full voice as the rugby mad public piled into their seats ready to see history. And they were duly rewarded before the blast of Matthew Carley’s whistle as Airlink provided not one but tw0 planes – one green for the Boks and one black for the visitors. Some might argue that the flyover at Ellis Park has become somewhat of a gimmick and doesn’t hit as hard as Lebombo did in 1995, but today, it felt fitting. Even before then, the 1996 captains – Gary Teichmann and Sean Fitzpatrick – of the last series between these two proud nations delivered their halves of the brand new trophy for the RGR. The latter was even embraced by Ardie Savea, as he held the New Zealand national flag during the anthem. Then there were the roars for the players’ names being read out, an even bigger one when Damian de Allende ran out for his 100th Test cap for the Springboks, accompanied by his family, before one of the best-ever renditions of Nkosi Sikelel’ iAfrika this writer has ever heard. As the final “In South Africa, our land” echoed through the stadium, it was time for the Haka, and as requested by Rassie Erasmus, Ellis Park remained as quiet as it could be as they enjoyed the spectacle. It was a fitting start to Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry at an iconic venue that means so much to this fixture, and that was before the first whistle. What ensued thereafter was a brutal, physical, skillful, tactical and truly epic battle between South Africa and New Zealand – which is what we’ve come to expect. All Blacks player ratings: ‘Predatory’ Will Jordan and ‘outstanding’ Jordie Barrett the linchpins while Dave Rennie ‘gets it right’ with big calls In the end, the All Blacks outscored the Springboks five tries to one, punishing the hosts’ indiscipline and inability to score points while being utterly ruthless with ball in hand. Will Jordan scored the first and last for New Zealand, with Josh Moorby, Fabian Holland and Luke Jacobson getting amongst the try-scorers too. Andre Esterhuizen battered his way over the line for South Africa’s sole try with Cheslin Koble kicking the remainder of the points. Just about every facet of this game was a contest except for one: the scrum. Frankly, it was men against boys as Ox Nche, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw shunted Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor and Tyrel Lomax backwards at an astonishing rate. It was a brutal obliteration for 54 minutes, during which time New Zealand boasted an atrocious 57% success rate. In the 55th minute, they finally got a penalty of their own – fortunately so – in their 22, but for the 54 minutes before then, it was a brutal demolition job not quite seen since the Boks battered Ireland’s set-piece. Losing De Groot before half-time didn’t help New Zealand’s cause in the scrums, nor did introducing George Bower, who replaced Lomax, who was completely outscrummaged by Nche. When the Boks made changes up front, there was somewhat of a levelling of the scrum battle, but the havoc Nche and Louw wreaked cannot be ignored. One thing is crystal clear: the All Blacks have to find some resemblance of scrum parity in Cape Town next week. They managed to escape a heap of trouble in the scrums, but they simply cannot afford to cough up possession and penalties in that manner for the rest of the series. There was a general feeling at half-time that the single-point advantage on the scoreboard that the Springboks held was not a true reflection of the encounter, as the hosts played in the right areas of the pitch, won several key battles as mentioned above, but when it came down to it, failed to capitalise on their opportunities. By the 64th minute, the Springboks had racked up nine entries into the All Blacks’ 22 but had a miserable 1.1 points per entry; in stark contrast, New Zealand had six entries into the Boks’ 22 and averaged 4.3 points. Springboks player ratings: ‘Human battering ram’ the shining light as several stars fail to fire in ‘humiliating’ All Blacks loss Time and time again, Erasmus’ men charged into New Zealand’s 22 and came up empty-handed whilst the All Blacks came away with points, living on the scraps gifted to them. Jordan’s score came through a gorgeous pass by Cam Roigard, who managed to catch the rapid Grant Williams somewhat flat-footed. Moorby also latched onto the final pass of a brilliant short-side attack. Holland was rather fortunate with his charge down, as it’s hard to believe that he was in fact behind the last man’s feet while Jacobson capitalised on some brilliant work off a scrum. While the Boks were wasteful, the All Blacks were ruthless, and that was the real difference today as Dave Rennie’s men go 1-0 up in the series. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Both coaches knew going into this game that they would not be able to retain the same matchday 23s across the four matches, and they were proven right, with both teams suffering hammer blows in this fixture. A nasty friendly-fire head clash took Josh Lord and De Groot in the first half, while the Boks lost Kurt-Lee Arendse, also to a head knock early on, which forced a backline reshuffle. Kolbe also did not look comfortable when he trotted off in the second half, as both coaches will hold their breath over the key players in their teams. Springboks scrum: How two words from Rassie Erasmus birthed the most feared set-piece in world rugby Erasmus stated that the series could be decided simply by who is left standing, and today’s brutality took its toll on both teams. Erasmus said before this match that while he hoped that his team would win the opener, it was not the most important Test match of the series – predicting that it would in fact be the third. Now, he and his counterpart, Rennie, have the opportunity to really get stuck into the analysis of their opposition. For the hosts, there is a major need to improve their ability to capitalise on their 22-metre entries, discpline and cut out the soft moments in defence. As for Rennie, he will be pleased with his side’s ruthlessness in attack, and ever-improving discipline. Next stop is the Cape Town Stadium, a venue that the Springboks have only lost once at – to the British and Irish Lions in 2021. The All Blacks get plenty of support in the Mother City and that will be a major positive but they will front up against a Springboks side that is hell-bent on levelling the series. title: Evaluating Anthony Richardson's performance v. Falcons in preseason - Yahoo Sports
content: With Riley Leonard getting the start for the Indianapolis Colts against the Atlanta Falcons, it was Anthony Richardson's turn to take over in the second half. So how did things go for Richardson in Week 2 of the preseason? Like Leonard, it was tough sledding through the air for Richardson as well. He finished the game completing just 3-of-9 passes for 24 yards at a lowly 2.7 yards per attempt. Not helping matters was the play of the offensive line unit, with Richardson facing regular pressure. And on several of Richardson's pass attempts, there appeared to be little separation between the Colts' wide receiver and the defensive back. That said, where he did differentiate himself was with his ability to extend plays. On a fourth-quarter drive into Falcons' territory, Richardson turned two near sacks into positive gains, picking up a first down in one instance. We also saw the Colts utilize more zone reads with Richardson, adding another element that defenses have to account for. I'll also add that when Richardson has been under duress, he's appeared more comfortable handling it this season. Shane Steichen said earlier this week that he doesn't have a timetable when it comes to making a decision on who the backup will be. From the outside looking in, it's been difficult to decipher up to this point who has the upper hand in this battle. That said, Richardson has had the better overall preseason performance over the last two weeks, and his mobility has helped set him a part, even when the passing game is sputtering. title: MATCH REPORT: All Blacks v Springboks, First Test | Rugby's Greatest Rivalry - All Blacks
content: It was a game fully representative of all 105 years of contact between the sides. Still, when it came down to tactical finesse, ball security and opportunities taken, the All Blacks enjoyed a five tries, two of them to wing Will Jordan, to one advantage. South Africa’s power game dominated the first 45 minutes of the contest, with the All Blacks scrum subjected to extreme pressure, yet South Africa couldn’t turn that into a game-winning points advantage. The All Blacks had only 39 percent territory across the game, but enjoyed a 56 percent possession advantage while winning 14 turnovers to five. By the end of the game, South Africa’s desperation resulted in two yellow cards in the last 10 minutes that allowed the All Blacks to finish the game in a canter. The much-feared Springbok bomb squad was not unleashed, and the box-kicking failed to give the home team the advantage they sought. They were happy to take points from penalty goals. But New Zealand’s defence, making 132 tackles to 86, denied the Springboks scoring chances, never more than when second five-eighths Jordie Barrett got his hand on a ball being carried by Springbok hooking powerhouse Malcolm Marx to force him to drop the ball in the act of diving for a try in the 36th minute. Then, after South Africa looked to take advantage of their soft-kick lobs over the All Blacks backs, a 47th-minute charge down by lock Fabian Holland of a clearing kick by halfback Grant Williams saw him reclaim the ball, sidestep first five-eighths Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and score. The All Blacks never conceded the lead from that point. The try coincided with the introduction of prop Fletcher Newell and hooker Asafo Aumua, a move that relieved the scrum pressure immediately but then turned it back on South Africa. Wing Cheslin Kolbe opened the scoring with a fourth-minute penalty goal, but the South Africans found themselves on the end of penalty errors, and the All Blacks made the most of it to get into Springbok territory. At a second lineout in the 22m area, after eight minutes, the All Blacks drove for halfback Cam Roigard to have a dart at the line. He was able to get back into position and fire a long pass in front of three All Blacks for Jordan to dive over in the corner. But All Blacks’ mistakes allowed the Springboks to reply similarly, using their lineout to move the ball wide, where replacement back Andre Esterhuizen burst through wing Josh Moorby’s tackle to cross in the 13th minute. The All Blacks had a chance as they got into the midfield in front of the posts, but Holland conceded a neck roll, and the Springboks cleared. However, the All Blacks kicked deep, and when Feinberg-Mngomezulu opted to take a mark in the 22m area, the All Blacks won the resulting lineout. Second five-eighths Jordie Barrett took the tackle in midfield, then was back in position when the ball was worked back to the blindside. His long pass found flanker Tupou Vaa’i on the sideline track where he got ahead to slip a pass inside to Moorby. He slipped a tackle and ran in for the try after 22 minutes. No sooner had they claimed the lead through first five-eighths Ruben Love’s sideline conversion than a penalty was conceded after the restart for Kolbe to land another penalty goal. South Africa returned deep into the All Blacks’ half but missed two scoring chances. Marx’s effort followed moments later when Feinberg-Mngomezulu opted for a cross-field kick that went directly to touch. The better option would have been to retain the ball, but that was reflective of the weaker decision-making by the Springboks throughout. The All Blacks were again under defensive pressure before the break, especially with lock Josh Lord and prop Ethan de Groot forced to leave the field after hitting heads in attempting a tackle. But the line held and halftime saw a 13-12 margin to the home team. Still, concern over penalties remains. In the first half, especially, the penalties favoured South Africa 4-9, which allowed them to get their big men, especially No8 Jasper Wiese, who was a handful every time he got the ball in his hands, and flanker Pieter-Steph du Toit, running hard and asking questions of the All Blacks defence. Another penalty goal was landed by Kolbe six minutes into the second half. However, Holland charged his kick down, recovered the ball, stepped Feinberg-Mngomezulu and scored. The momentum changed, and the All Blacks took control in the most emphatic result in recent New Zealand history. South Africa 16 (Andre Esterhuizen try; Cheslin Kolbe con, 3 pen) New Zealand 33 (Will Jordan 2, Josh Moorby, Fabian Holland, Luke Jacobson tries; Ruben Love 4 con). HT: 13-12

title: Brentford 3-0 Spurs: How the players rated - BBC
content: Brentford made it a miserable start to the Premier League season for Roberto de Zerbi's expensively rebuilt Tottenham Hotspur side with an emphatic 3-0 victory at The Gtech Community Stadium. Here's how I rated the players and how you rated the players. Spurs make nightmare start as Brentford hit three in easy win Caoimhin Kelleher: Calm as ever in goal and made the saves when he needed to. 6 Michael Kayode: Busy and a threat out wide. Opportunist goal to effectively clinch the victory. 7 Kristoffer Ajer: Read the game well throughout. Composed and dealt well with any Spurs danger there was. 6 Nathan Collins: Missed early headed chance but it did not prove costly. Untroubled at the back. 6 Keane Lewis-Potter: Clinical finish for Brentford's opening goal and provided quality on the flanks. 7 Vitaly Janelt: Pounced for second goal and provided the sort of solid performance Brentford have come to count on. 7 Mathias Jensen: Dangerous from set-pieces and his shot helped set up Brentford's second goal for Janelt. 7 Dango Ouattara: Poor touch cost him a chance of a goal in the first half but his prodigious work-rate made a crucial contribution. 6 Mamadou Sangare: Outstanding. Won possession, used possession and set up Lewis-Potter's opening goal superbly. Club-record signing at £39m looks a bargain. 8 Igor Thiago: Physical presence worried Spurs. Marred an excellent performance by missing a second-half penalty. 7 Kevin Schade: Always looking to link with Thiago and worried the Spurs defence throughout. 6 Yehor Yarmoliuk (on 67, Jensen): Eased his way into the action.5 Jaidon Anthony (on 67, Ouattara): Quiet introduction for debutant. 5 Subs not used: Valdimarsson,, Henry, Pinnock, Schuster. Antonin Kinsky: Bad day for Spurs' new first-choice goalkeeper. Was at fault when he pushed out Jensen's shot for Janelt's goal. Distribution wayward. 5 Archie Gray: The youngest captain in Spurs history but not a day for celebration. Played as an emergency right-back and looked like, well, an emergency right-back. 5 Marcos Senesi: Struggled to cope with the physical presence of Igor Thiago and the movement of those around Brentford's Brazilian striker. 5 Jan Paul van Hecke: For Senesi read Van Hecke. Never comfortable in a shambolic Spurs defence. 5 Andrew Robertson: Tough debut for the veteran left-back. Struggled to cope with Brentford's pace and movement on the right flank. 5 Conor Gallagher: Took a couple of heavy early knocks and had a wild shot off target. Booked for trip on Sangare and no surprise when he was replaced at half-time. 4 Lucas Bergvall: Too many wasted passes and gave away possession poorly for Brentford's second goal. 4 Sandro Tonali: Desperately poor debut for Spurs' £100m signing. title: Michael Wright, Star of ‘The Five Heartbeats’ and ‘V,’ Dies at 70 - TheWrap
content: The actor’s wife says his “work will live forever” and he “will be missed beyond words” Michael Wright, the actor best known for starring in “The Five Heartbeats” and “V,” has died. He was 70 years old. Wright’s wife Susan Wright shared the news on Instagram late Friday, writing that his “work will live forever” and he “will be missed beyond words.” “It is with profound sadness and an unimaginable heaviness in my heart that I share the passing of my beloved husband, Michael Wright,” Susan wrote. “Michael was a husband, a father (Manon Wright, Byron Barr, Brittney Briggs, Brianna Barr, Sir Barr), a grandfather (Yoko), loved one, a friend and an extraordinary artist whose work touched generations. “Many knew and loved him through ‘The Five Heartbeats,’ ‘The Wanderers,’ ‘V,’ ‘The Principal,’ ‘Streamers’ and the many other characters he brought to life throughout his remarkable career. His talent, presence, and contributions to film and television will live on, but to those of us who loved him personally, he was so much more than the roles the world knew him for.” The actor died Wednesday in Los Angeles after complications from a rare degenerative neurological disease, called Marchiafava-Bignami, sent him into heart failure, the Wright family told TMZ in a statement. Michael Wright’s first film role was 1979’s “The Wanderers,” but his breakout came with 1983 limited series “V,” starring as Elias Taylor. He reprised the role for the sci-fi drama’s 1984 follow-up “V: The Final Battle” and from 1984–85 in the “V” television series. According to IMDb, Wright’s final role was in 2025’s “Dope King.” In her announcement of his passing Friday, Susan Wright wrote, “Our family is grieving an enormous and deeply personal loss. We understand how much Michael meant to so many people, and we are grateful for the love, prayers, memories and condolences already being shared.” She asked the public and news media to allow “privacy and grace” as they grieve Michael’s death and said to expect more information “regarding Michael’s life, legacy, and how we intend to honor and celebrate him” in the coming days. “Michael, your work will live forever, but your love will live even longer in the hearts of those who knew you best,” Susan concluded. “Rest peacefully, my love. You will be missed beyond words.” Michael is survived by his wife Susan, five children and a grandchild.

title: Michael Wright, The Five Heartbeats and V star, dies aged 70 - RTE.ie
content:
The family of The Five Heartbeats actor Michael Wright are "grieving an enormous and deeply personal loss" following his death aged 70. Wright's death was confirmed by his wife, Susan Wright, in a statement on Instagram. The statement began: "It is with profound sadness and an unimaginable heaviness in my heart that I share the passing of my beloved husband, Michael Wright. "Michael was a husband, a father (Manon Wright, Byron Barr, Brittney Briggs, Brianna Barr, Sir Barr, a grandfather (Yoko), loved one, a friend, and an extraordinary artist whose work touched generations. "Many knew and loved him through The Five Heartbeats, The Wanderers, V, The Principal, Streamers, and the many other characters he brought to life throughout his remarkable career." It continued: "His talent, presence, and contributions to film and television will live on, but to those of us who loved him personally, he was so much more than the roles the world knew him for." The statement said Wright's family were "grieving an enormous and deeply personal loss". The family said they understood how much the actor had "meant to so many people and were grateful for the love, prayers, memories, and condolences already being shared". However, they asked to be given "privacy and grace to grieve during this incredibly difficult time". They said they would share additional information regarding Wright's "life, legacy and how we intend to honour and celebrate him" in the coming days. The statement, which was signed by his "loving wife and family", concluded: "Michael, your work will live forever, but your love will live even longer in the hearts of those who knew you best. Rest peacefully, my love. You will be missed beyond words." Born in New York City in 1956, Wright appeared in more than 50 films and television shows throughout his career. His breakout role came as Clinton, the leader of the Del Bombers gang, in Philip Kaufman's 1979 coming-of-age drama The Wanderers. The film was adapted from Richard Price's novel of the same name and followed rival teenage gangs in 1960s New York. Wright went on to play singer Eddie King Jr in Robert Townsend's 1991 film The Five Heartbeats.> The cult favourite followed a fictional Motown group but was loosely inspired by the lives of artists including The Temptations, James Brown, and Sam Cooke. Wright also appeared in Robert Altman's 1983 war drama Streamers and Leon Ichaso's 1995 crime drama Sugar Hill, in which he starred opposite Wesley Snipes. On the small screen, some of Wright's best-known roles included playing Elias Taylor in V and V: The Series, Omar White in Oz, and Lazarus Prime in Black Lightning. © RTÉ 2026. title: AFC Wimbledon v Reading: League One stats & head-to-head - BBC
content: AFC Wimbledon and Reading ground out a stalemate at Plough Lane in a game of few chances. In the first real attack of the contest, Jack Marriott forced keeper Joe McDonnell to palm away his shot across the face of goal after 14 minutes. The visitors looked more potent up front, although without really creating a clear-cut opportunity. Reading almost opened the scoring five minutes after the restart when Josh Stokes saw close-range efforts blocked by McDonnell, and Dan Sweeney denied Kyreece Lisbie from the follow-up. The home side slowly got into the game, having withstood some more Reading pressure, and Ryan Johnson saw his 68th-minute effort cleared off the line after a Zack Nelson free-kick. With five minutes' additional time, it was likely one chance would decide the game. However, despite a late run by Steven Sessegnon for the hosts, it proved honours even. AFC Wimbledon won each of their two league games against Reading last season, in the EFL they’ve only beaten three sides in each of their first three matches against them – Colchester United, Notts County and York City. Reading have lost six of their last seven away league games against sides from London (D1), conceding 2.3 goals on average per fixture across that time. Only twice before have AFC Wimbledon lost each of their opening two games of a Football League season, in 2016-17 and 2019-20, though both came at the third tier level. Reading lost their League One opener 4-3 against Luton, the Royals last conceded 3+ goals in each of their opening two matches of an EFL campaign in 1998-99 when they lost 0-3 to Wrexham and then 4-1 to Bristol Rovers. title: Who will start at quarterback for Colts in preseason game v. Falcons? - Yahoo Sports
content: Who will start at quarterback for the Indianapolis Colts in the team's Week 2 preseason matchup with the Atlanta Falcons? Early in the week, Shane Steichen announced that the Colts starters wouldn't be playing in this game, paving the way for Riley Leonard to get the start. As Leonard competes with Anthony Richardson for the backup quarterback role, the two have alternated starting opportunities in the preseason up to this point. With Richardson getting the start against New England, it is now Leonard's turn. Richardson will then take over in the second half, just as Leonard did a week ago. From the outside looking in, it's difficult to decipher who has the upper hand in this battle. As Steichen said on Thursday, both quarterbacks have flashed, but each has had thier ups and downs as well. "I thought they both had a good camp," Steichen said, via The Indy Star's Nathan Brown. As of now, Steichen didn't put a timetable on when he plans on making a decision. This competition may be close, but perhaps there's a little more extra pressure on Leonard this week, with Richardson having the better performance in Week 1. title: BMW and Kith Team Up to Build an E53 X5 SUV with 10 Cylinders and a Manual Transmission - Car and Driver
content: The first X5 correctly predicted the popularity of crossovers, and this one is as appealing as they get. It seems hard to think that any crossover could age into being a modern classic, but if one has, it's the E53-chassis BMW X5. Launched in 1999, it was a pioneer for the idea of a performance-oriented SUV, aiming to blend the poise and punch of the 5-series sedan with greater capability in all conditions. Not just a forerunner of a rising trend, this generation of X5 has also aged extremely well in the styling department, especially when compared with the warthog-from-the-Lion King looks of the current XM. However, like any car that's over two decades old, a bit of a refresh and a tidy-up is needed to keep them on the road. And if you're going to be taking things apart anyway, why not build the kind of X5 that BMW was never brave enough to sell to the public? This 2000 X5 was completely torn down and restored, and then built back up with V-10 power plucked from a BMW M5. It belongs to Ronnie Fieg, a successful entrepreneur in New York's sneaker and urban-wear scene and lifelong fan of the Knicks. He's also a longtime BMW fan, and his Kith NYC brand previously worked with BMW to craft a limited-edition version of the M4 Competition. The ultimate E53 is, of course, the insane X5 Le Mans, a one-off prototype that BMW shoved the V-12 from the McLaren F1 into. Complete lunacy, but it does emphasize that BMW's motorsports division must have been a pretty fun place to work in the early 2000s. Kith's V-10-powered X5 has a new front end that's inspired by that X5 LM, with a widebody kit and rear aero treatment to match. It rides a little lower on a reworked suspension, but the look is pretty subtle. Visually, this X5 could basically be OEM. Technically, so could the powertrain. The most powerful versions of the X5 got some punchy V-8s, but in its last year of production, 2006, BMW brought out the 10-cylinder M5 and M6. The engine here isn't quite stock, having been built up with forged pistons and some custom tuning, but it's again a subtle massaging rather than a SEMA-style show-off build. The interior sews it all together with an entirely factory look if you didn't spot the 9000-rpm tachometer (taken from the M5). Best detail: the stick-shift transmission between the seats. Yes, this is a proper three-pedal manual transmission, paired with a 500-hp 5.0-liter V-10 and retaining the factory all-wheel-drive system. It should be an absolute hoot to drive, and while plenty of customizing was required to get everything to fit, it largely contains parts right out of the BMW catalog. V-10 power in an X5? What might have been. Only a one-off, this project nonetheless raises the profile of the E53 X5 a little, to the point that collectors looking around for something cool but affordable might notice. With the X5, BMW set out to predict the future, and it mostly got it right. Building a potential collectible while doing so is something of a happy accident. title: Is South Africa v New Zealand on TV? Channel, kick-off time and how to watch first Test - Yahoo Sports
content: South Africa and New Zealand collide in the first of four huge Tests in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series. The All Blacks have won all three of their warm-up games since arriving in South Africa, and now take on a Springboks side that beat them in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final. Rassie Erasmus' world champions are unbeaten in their last 12 matches and were narrow victors in the pair's last encounter at Ellis Park. Another blockbuster encounter could be in store as the landmark series launches in style. The first Test is due to kick off at 4.10pm BST on Saturday 22 August at Ellis Park in Johannesburg. Viewers in the United Kingdom can watch every game from the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry tour live on Sky Sports, while South African viewers can tune in via SuperSport. Siya Kolisi is left out by the Springboks, with Paul de Villiers preferred on the openside as South Africa take a cautious approach with their captain. title: Actor Michael Wright, Star of ‘The Five Heartbeats’ and ‘V,’ Dies at 70 - Variety
content:
Michael Wright, an actor known for his roles in “The Five Heartbeats,” “Streamers,” “The Principal” and “V,” has died, according to a statement from his family. He was 70. His wife, Susan Wright, announced his death in a post shared Friday evening on Instagram. “It is with profound sadness and an unimaginable heaviness in my heart that I share the passing of my beloved husband, Michael Wright,” her statement read. Wright’s family said he died in Los Angeles on Wednesday, Aug. 19, after suffering heart failure coupled with complications of degenerative neurological disease Marchiafava-Bignami, according to a statement provided to TMZ. Wright was born on April 30, 1956, in New York City. He appeared in more than 50 movies and TV shows, including the films “The Five Heartbeats,” Robert Altman’s Vietnam drama “Streamers,” “Sugar Hill” and “The Wanderers.” His TV credits include the 1980s sci-fi series “V” and HBO’s “Oz.” In the Robert Townsend-directed 1991 musical film “The Five Heartbeats,” about a fictional Motown group, Wright played the band’s charismatic lead vocalist, Eddie King Jr., whose alcohol and drug addiction forces him to leave the Heartbeats. “Michael was a husband, a father (Manon Wright, Byron Barr, Brittney Briggs, Brianna Barr, Sir Barr, a grandfather (Yoko), loved one, a friend, and an extraordinary artist whose work touched generations,” Susan’s statement said. “Many knew and loved him through ‘The Five Heartbeats,’ ‘The Wanderers,’ ‘V,’ ‘The Principal,’ ‘Streamers,’ and the many other characters he brought to life throughout his remarkable career. His talent, presence, and contributions to film and television will live on, but to those of us who loved him personally, he was so much more than the roles the world knew him for.” Her statement continued, “Our family is grieving an enormous and deeply personal loss. We understand how much Michael meant to so many people, and we are grateful for the love, prayers, memories, and condolences already being shared. … In the coming days, when we are ready, we will share additional information regarding Michael’s life, legacy, and how we intend to honor and celebrate him.” Susan concluded, “Michael, your work will live forever, but your love will live even longer in the hearts of those who knew you best. Rest peacefully, my love. You will be missed beyond words.” In a 2021 interview with Sheen Magazine, Wright said, “The greatest sin an actor can commit is to fail to be interesting. I always try to make my characters interesting. I want you to be riveted and wonder what’s going on behind my eyes.” Wright also said there wasn’t anything in his life he would do over: “I’ve done everything I have wanted to do. I’ve been everywhere, I speak five different languages. I have seen the world; I love my experiences.” 3 Comments Comments are moderated. content: Wigan fell to two defeats from two in League One as Leyton Orient won 2-0 at the Brick Community Stadium. The home side almost fell behind in the opening exchanges when an Orient counter attack was only ruined by a desperately poor final ball into the unmarked Jaze Kabia. Gary Caldwell's men did not heed the warning, however, and Orient took the lead after 15 minutes when Wigan failed to clear their lines and Tony Springett fired home from close range. Wigan came close to a leveller when Dara Costelloe chased what looked to be a lost cause and forced the error from the last defender, only to lob the ball over Nathan Baxter but on to the roof of the net. On-loan Chelsea midfielder Reggie Walsh thought he had scored on his Wigan debut with a cracking volley from 15 yards, only to be denied by an offside flag. After Costelloe fired just wide of the target from the edge of the box, Orient doubled their lead after 58 minutes when a horrible mistake by Jon Mellish was punished by Yusuf Akhamrich from 10 yards. Wigan threw on five substitutes in the final half an hour to try to get into it, and one of them – Chris Sze – almost scored with his first touch, only to be denied by Orient's replacement goalkeeper Noah Phillips. Leyton Orient have kept clean sheets in each of their last two away league games against Wigan Athletic and will be looking to keep three in succession for the first time. Despite defeat to Cambridge on the opening day of the 2026-27 League One season, Wigan led all sides in the competition for total xG (3.04). It was their third-largest tally on Opta record (since 2019-20), after amassing 3.45 vs Bristol Rovers in September 2024 and 3.06 vs Rotherham in August 2025. title: Auntie v influencers: why YouTubers are ready for battle with the BBC - The Guardian
content: Content creators are fighting proposal to boost traditional broadcasters in video platforms’ all-powerful algorithms The millions who subscribe to the content creator Simon Squibb’s social media channels are usually delivered tips and hacks on how to turn their dream business idea into reality. But they were recently presented with something completely different. In an Instagram post entitled “the government wants to control YOU”, Squibb issued an urgent call to arms. He asked his followers to fight against a proposal that he said could force content from the BBC and other traditional broadcasters into their social media feeds and recommendations whether they liked it or not. Squibb is one of many major UK content creators outraged by a proposal included in a government paper earlier in the summer that would boost content from traditional broadcasters such as the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 in the all-powerful algorithms of YouTube and TikTok. The idea has been pushed collectively by public service broadcasters as a way of boosting trusted material and preserving distinctly British content. Ministers want to help them survive in a world in which audiences are ditching traditional TV for digital platforms. They prefer a voluntary deal with digital platforms, but have pointed to using legislation if necessary. Video-sharing platforms and streaming services accounted for 74% of all video time for audiences aged 16-24 in 2024-25, and 69% for 25-34s. YouTube is the most-watched service for children aged four to 15, accounting for 28% of their video viewing. But the measure has slowly but surely been causing anger and disbelief among content creators, who see it as shifting the goalposts to allow bigger players to stay on top. If the broadcasters go up the algorithm, they reason content creators will be pushed down. They have been holding private meetings, putting out emergency videos and urging viewers and fellow creators to speak out before the government’s consultation ends at the end of the month, featuring dramatic warnings about “the end of YouTube”. Squibb and others have even raised comparisons with authoritarian state control. “Russia pushes its channels that it believes the people should watch,” he said. “I just think it’s a very bad thing to push. Trust has to be earned. If the BBC is selected as one of the trusted sources, does that also mean that Dragons’ Den is going to get prominent coverage over my education and business content? You have to let the public decide.” Ben Ebbrell, whose Sorted Food channel started as a small project among friends and now has 15 million viewers tuning in each month, said the idea would undermine 16 years of investment in building an audience, a period in which the TV world ignored the growing popularity of YouTube, he said. “At first, the TV world almost looked down upon content creators, but it’s completely flipped now, where we feel like we’ve got the stardust. “It was just quite a shock when they said almost that they didn’t want to start playing the game, they wanted to move goalposts – or possibly even running off the pitch with a ball and a bit of a sulk … it’s kind of embarrassing.” Jade Beason, a creator with 310,000 YouTube subscribers who has worked with traditional broadcasters on their digital content, said they should concentrate instead on making content that works for digital platforms – something the BBC and others are trying to do. “I don’t think it’s going to get them the results that they need and I think it’s going to disrupt creators in the process,” she said. “To me, it just feels like you’re pushing the queue, you’re jumping ahead. “[Traditional broadcasters] don’t need more help for people to find them … people aren’t struggling to find TV news, they know where it is. They’re choosing not to watch it. That’s the challenge we should be focusing on.” Grace Andrews, a content creator who helped set up the Diary of a CEO podcast, is among those coordinating the pushback against the idea and rounding up responses before the end of the month. YouTube has also been encouraging creators to respond. “Now obviously [traditional broadcasters] are scrambling for eyeballs and instead of adapting to that world, they’re trying to legislate their way back into it,” she said. “Nobody who actually understands why people watch what they watch in 2026 was in the room when this document was created. “I don’t want misinformation on my feeds either, but I don’t think this is the solution. Social media works because people are choosing what they see. That’s the entire mechanic. The second that becomes something enforced instead of something they picked, they don’t trust it any more.” A spokesperson for the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said: “We want to ensure that content from public service media providers such as the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and others is easily discoverable on video-sharing platforms, like YouTube, and we have urged the industry to come together and move quickly on voluntary solutions. “We do not see this as a zero-sum game between traditional broadcasters, content creators and other video platforms. We want to create an environment where PSM [public service media] providers, high-quality news providers and content creators can all thrive.”

title: Cowboys v. Cardinals: 5 Players to Watch - Inside The Star
content: Over the last few days, I’ve broken down a few position groups on the Cowboys roster and tried to get a better feel for where some of these battles stand. This time, I’m narrowing it down to a few individual players worth watching tonight when Dallas takes on the Arizona Cardinals in preseason game 2. Saturday night is about the guys Dallas still has decisions to make on. I have Camden Brown making this list easily after what he did against Seattle. The undrafted rookie caught three passes for 62 yards and two touchdowns in the opener, and he has become one of the biggest talking points coming out of that game. I know we can all see why. It’s because that’s what happens when you’re fighting for a roster spot and make the most of the few opportunities you get. I’m not expecting him to go out and score two touchdowns again, but I do want to see if he can keep the production going. He needs separation from Jonathan Mingo. I want to see him make the routine catches and if he can just keep looking like a player who deserves a spot on the 53. The bottom of the depth chart is crowded at receiver, but Brown is making it hard to ignore him. Malachi Lawrence is someone we have all been keeping tabs on. That’s what happens when you’re a first round pick, but the part I’m paying attention to is his first step. I’ve covered that the Cowboys have been working with him on getting rid of that false step off the snap. It doesn’t sound like much, but when you’re trying to beat NFL tackles around the edge, that little bit of wasted movement can be the difference between pressure and getting washed out. He didn’t record a sack against the Seahawks, and that’s OK. Lawrence has the size and speed combo a team covets. Now I want to see if some of those smaller technical things are starting to show up. Jaishawn Barham might be the most interesting player on the field Saturday, if he gets on the field. He’s flashed in camp, especially when it comes to getting off blocks and playing downhill. Dallas also likes the fact he can do more than one thing for the defense. The way I see it is, camp is one thing. I want to see what happens when the play breaks down in live action. How will he respond? Will he be able to handle the ugly stuff that comes when playing in a real game? I want to see if he can find the ball in traffic, can he get away from a lineman once they get their hands on him, and how will he hold up in space? If Barham handles those situations well, Dallas may have to find more snaps for this player. Maybe even a starting role. I thought about putting Sam Howell here, but I think his NFL starting experience will put him above Joe Milton, but this player is still the more interesting player. Against Seattle, Milton was efficient and didn’t try to turn every throw into a highlight reel. I want to watch and see if he continues to take the easy throws for completions, and if he can keep the offense moving even when he’s in trouble. A player in his position has to understand what the offense wants. That type of football could be what helps him take over QB2 from Sam Howell. Joe Milton needs to finish out the preseason with clean, efficient games to prove he has slowed down. If Milton looks steady again, Howell is going to have to earn QB2. title: Sutton's predictions: Brentford v Tottenham - Yahoo Sports
content: There is a lot of excitement surrounding Tottenham and I understand why. Sandro Tonali is an excellent signing for them in midfield while, at the back, Marcos Senesi and Jan Paul van Hecke are both very good defenders and Micky van de Ven has penned a new deal too. I am really looking forward to seeing Spurs under Roberto de Zerbi and the expectation will be that they do well. Without European football, they must be thinking about the top six. Keith Andrews had a sensational first season as Brentford manager and it will be interesting to see how they set up - will it be a case of 'counter-attack Keith' again? The way I see this game going, Spurs will have most of the ball but Brentford are well organised and very dangerous on the break. Igor Thiago had an incredible campaign for the Bees last time and they have got Kevin Schade too, so I don't see them struggling for goals.

title: Sutton's predictions: Ipswich Town v Sunderland - Yahoo Sports
content: I must point out that Ipswich boss Gary O'Neil is a former Norwich player, so where do his loyalties really lie? And has he gone to Ipswich to sabotage them? Seriously though, I wish him well and I genuinely hope for East Anglia that Ipswich can make a decent fist of it and stay up. I really like some of their signings too - Daizen Maeda is a player I know well and is a really good piece of business, coming in from Celtic. Maeda plays with such intensity. He will be the best pressing player in the Premier League bar none and, if you want to play on the counter-attack and you want someone to run in behind, there are not many quicker than him. Seeing what Sunderland did last season, when they also signed lots of players after getting promoted, will give Ipswich hope. Ditto with Leeds, who also recruited well. But then it is about knitting the new players together and connecting early on. That has to be O'Neil's aim, but it will be difficult. Sunderland did so well they qualified for Europe, and I am not sure how their squad will cope with the extra games. For now, though, I think they will remind us of how good they were last season. Like I said on Monday Night Club, I never saw another team beat Arsenal up the way they did. They faded as the campaign went on and they are not going to surprise anyone this time, but they still have the leadership of Granit Xhaka in midfield and Wilson Isidor and Brian Brobbey up top to hurt teams.

title: Sutton's predictions: Everton v Crystal Palace - Yahoo Sports
content: After the success Oliver Glasner had at Crystal Palace, new boss Pierre Sage has got some big shoes to fill. Still, Palace have got some serious firepower and plenty of goals in their team, so I think they will be fine this season. Goals are a bigger problem for Everton and again the key to their campaign probably rests on what manager David Moyes can get out of strikers Thierno Barry and Beto. But I am sure Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall will chip in too because he is a wonderful footballer and, while I do see Palace scoring, I fancy Everton to edge this.

title: UND Law Professor Carolyn V. Williams Receives 2026 Outstanding Service Award - University of North Dakota (UND)
content: Updates from the University of North Dakota School of Law. University of North Dakota School of Law Professor Carolyn V. Williams has received the 2026 Outstanding Service Award from the Association of Legal Writing Directors (ALWD). The ALWD Board of Directors voted unanimously to recognize Williams for her work as author of the eighth edition of the ALWD Guide to Legal Citation. In announcing the award, the Board highlighted not only the extensive work involved in revising the Guide, but also Williams’s efforts to engage the legal writing community in developing new rules addressing the use and citation of generative artificial intelligence. The Board praised Williams for developing “common-sense and functional AI rules” and for her work promoting the Guide as a citation resource for law students, professors, lawyers, and judges. ALWD is a national professional organization dedicated to advancing legal writing and supporting legal writing professionals as teachers, scholars, and leaders. Among its major initiatives, ALWD publishes the ALWD Guide to Legal Citation, a nationally used legal citation manual designed to make citation clear, accessible, and practical for students and practicing lawyers alike. The Guide also plays an important role in supporting ALWD’s broader mission, including by helping to fund a range of programs and initiatives that support legal writing faculty in developing innovative teaching materials and pursuing scholarly projects. Williams authored both the seventh and eighth editions of the Guide. The newly released eighth edition includes substantial updates reflecting changes in legal research and practice, including a new rule addressing when and how lawyers and legal scholars should acknowledge or cite the use of generative AI. Following completion of the eighth edition, Williams was also hired as a consultant by LexisNexis to revise and rewrite its Interactive Citation Workshop exercises for the ALWD Guide, ensuring that the online exercises used by law students and legal writing professors align with the eighth edition’s updated rules and citation standards. Williams will be formally recognized for the Outstanding Service Award at ALWD’s 2027 Biennial Conference. title: DC’s ‘People v. Gorilla Grodd’ Mockumentary Series Set at HBO Max, Skyler Gisondo and Jimmy Tatro to Star - Variety
content:
"American Vandal" creators Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault will serve as showrunners HBO Max is officially moving forward with their DC Studios mockumentary series, now titled “The People v. Gorilla Grodd.” The show was first reported to be in the works in November 2025. As reported at the time, Skyler Gisondo will reprise the role of Jimmy Olsen, whom he first played in the 2025 “Superman” movie. Jimmy Tatro is officially set to play Gorilla Grodd. HBO Max has given the show an eight-episode order. The logline for the show states, “A superintelligent ape (Tatro) is convicted of murdering his father, the King of Gorilla City. In an eight-part ‘true’ crime docuseries, the Daily Planet’s Jimmy Olsen (Gisondo) reopens the case, investigating whether Gorilla Grodd was wrongly convicted in one of Metropolis’ most famous murder trials.” Along with Gisondo and Tatro, the series will also star “Superman” actors Beck Bennett as Steve Lombard, Mikaela Hoover as Cat Grant, and Wendell Pierce as Perry White. Additional cast members include Mary Holland, Eduardo Franco, Arian Moayed, Andrew Leeds, and Tim Baltz. Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault will serve as writers, executive producers, and showrunners on the series, with Perrault also set as part of the show’s cast. Yacenda will direct all eight episodes. James Gunn and Peter Safran also executive produce. DC Studios and Warner Bros. Television will produce. “We’re excited by the challenge of creating a series that feels less like an entry into the DCU and more like an artifact from it,” Yacenda and Perrault said. “A Daily Planet original documentary made for the people of Metropolis. We hope it’ll appeal to fans of the comics, comedy and true crime. And while we can’t speak for audiences here yet, we already know it’s a huge hit in Metropolis. They love this series.” Yacenda and Perrault are no strangers to the world of mockumentary series. The duo famously created the critically-acclaimed Netflix show “American Vandal,” which spoofed the true crime genre. The show aired for two seasons at the streamer and won a Peabody Award for its first season in addition to being nominated for an Emmy for best writing for a comedy series. Tatro and Franco both starred in the show’s first season. Yacenda and Perrault then went on to create the Paramount+ mockumentary series “Players,” which was set in the world of eSports. title: Hyundai's Ioniq V Looks Like A Lambo, Is As Big As A Camry, And Costs Less Than America's Cheapest New Car - Carscoops
content:
At 193 inches long for Venue money, this cyberpunk electric sedan makes Western EV pricing hard to defend When Hyundai launched the original Ioniq Hybrid in America in 2017, it started at $22,200. Almost a decade later, Chinese buyers can order an entirely new, fully electric Ioniq sedan for less. The wedgy Ioniq V has entered pre-sales at just 119,900 yuan, which equates to only $17,800 at current exchange rates. That’s nearly $3,000 less than the cheapest new car in America right now, which also happens to be a Hyundai, the Venue. That’s for the Standard Edition. Upping the spend to 129,900 yuan ($19,300) gets the Smart Driving Edition, while 139,900 yuan ($20,800) buys the Long Range model, Auto Home reports. Those are some startling numbers when viewed from America or Europe, and remind us how cutthroat the competition is in the Chinese car market. Related: Police Are Slipping Warning Cards Under Hyundai And Kia Wipers Again The Ioniq V is a China-focused model developed under Beijing Hyundai, and despite what the prices suggest, it’s no cramped subcompact. At 4,900 mm (193 inches) long with a 2,900 mm (114-inch) wheelbase, it occupies roughly the same footprint as a Hyundai Sonata or a Toyota Camry. The Sonata measures 193.3 inches long on a 111.8-inch wheelbase; the Camry 193.5 inches on a 111.2-inch wheelbase. The Ioniq V wraps frameless doors and fastback proportions around some properly cyberpunk styling, and the paint chart runs eight colors deep, well past the silvers and grays Western buyers get stuck with. Cyber Gold, Gamma Green and a funky Dimensional Purple are all on the list. Inside, there’s a vast 27-inch 4K display running Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295 chip, plus a head-up display. Hyundai has also thrown Chinese AI models from Baidu and ByteDance into the infotainment system, while Momenta supplies the driver-assistance technology. Hyundai’s site additionally boasts nine airbags and extensive active safety equipment. Power comes from a single electric motor with either 188 hp (191 PS / 140 kW) or 225 hp (228 PS / 178 kW). CATL supplies 53.5 kWh and 66.8 kWh LFP batteries, producing four claimed CLTC ranges spanning 323 to 404 miles (520 to 650 km). Those optimistic Chinese-cycle numbers don’t translate directly into equivalent EPA range, naturally, but even if they’re 20 percent lower the value proposition is difficult to ignore. There’s no guarantee the Ioniq V will ever reach Western showrooms, much less at anything resembling Chinese pricing. Or that Hyundai will ever create the N version to capitalize on that Lamborghini-esque design, even though our own renders suggest it would look fantastic. But $17,800 for a brand-new electric sedan this stylish sounds like a great deal whichever side of the Pacific you’re on. title: 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid vs. Hyundai Tucson Hybrid: Which Is the Better Buy? - GreenCars
content: By using this site, you consent to our and our third-party partners use of cookies and similar technologies, including for advertising, analytics, and other purposes. Please see our Privacy Policy for more details. ⚙️ Output: The CR-V Hybrid makes 204 horsepower, while the Tucson Hybrid makes 231 horsepower 🚗 Drivetrain: Both the CR-V Hybrid and Tucson Hybrid offer front- or all-wheel drive ⛽ Fuel Economy (EPA estimated): The CR-V Hybrid gets up to 40 mpg combined, while the Tucson Hybrid gets up to 38 mpg combined 🖥️ Tech: The CR-V Hybrid gets a 9.0-inch touchscreen, while the Tucson Hybrid gets a 12.3-inch touchscreen 🧳 Cargo: The CR-V Hybrid holds 36.3 cu ft behind the second row, while the Tucson Hybrid holds 41.2 cu ft 💰MSRP: The CR-V Hybrid starts at an MSRP of $37,080, while the Tucson Hybrid starts at an MSRP of $32,950 The small SUV market typically isn’t the most exciting segment to talk about, but it's the one Americans are most likely to gravitate toward. These smaller utilities account for 19 percent of the market so far in 2026, with 37 percent more sales than full-size pickups. In 2025, Honda sold more than 200,000 CR-V Hybrids, making it one of the bestselling small hybrid SUVs on the market. The Hyundai Tucson Hybrid’s sales figures are quite a bit smaller than that, but they've grown considerably over the past few years. Honda offers the CR-V in both hybrid and nonhybrid powertrains, while Hyundai adds a plug-in variant to the Tucson lineup. The Honda CR-V Hybrid's last redesign was in 2023. It’s not an old design, but with so many sales, it’s a pretty familiar sight almost anywhere you go. Honda really wants to emphasize the “s” in SUV, as all four of its hybrid trim levels tout “sport” in one way or another. All jokes aside, it’s a stylish vehicle with a design that leans more toward classic and timeless than trendy and bold. For a deeper look at Honda’s comfort, efficiency, and everyday driving experience, see how the top-spec CR-V Hybrid performs in a full road test ➜ The Tucson Hybrid’s design is quite different and leans toward the latter of that description. It takes on a rounded shape, a large front grille, and sharp lines and dimensional carvings down the side of the vehicle. It's without a doubt sportier than its predecessor, but its design might be a little bold for some drivers. These two small hybrid SUVs are pretty competitive in size. You’ll only find an inch of difference or less between most of their measurements. The only notable gap comes in the cargo hold, where the Tucson Hybrid has slightly more space than the CR-V Hybrid. So if you’re packing a double stroller or you're a regular visitor to your local big box store, you might find the Tucson Hybrid a bit more flexible. Both vehicles come standard with cloth upholstery, dual climate controls, USB-C charging ports, and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. The Tucson Hybrid’s 12.3-inch touchscreen dwarfs the Honda’s 9.0-inch. Heated front seats, a power moonroof, and a power driver’s seat are standard on the CR-V Hybrid but are upgrades on the Tucson Hybrid. Both can be had with leather upholstery, a wireless charging pad, a Bose premium sound system, a heated steering wheel, a power liftgate, and driver's seat memory settings. If ventilated front seats or heated rear seats are on your must-have list, you won’t find them on the CR-V Hybrid’s list of available features. The Tucson Hybrid offers those, plus some other niceties like a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster and a 12-inch head-up display. The Honda also offers an upgraded 10.2-inch digital instrument cluster, but overall, its list of available features is shorter than what’s offered in the Hyundai. As far as safety suites go, both have a standard driver-assist suite that includes adaptive cruise control, blind-spot monitoring, automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping assist, lane-following assist, driver-attention warning, rear-occupant alert, and rear cross-traffic alert. The Tucson Hybrid’s standard suite also includes safe-exit assist, while the CR-V Hybrid's includes traffic-sign recognition. The Tucson Hybrid can be had with forward-attention warning, a blind-spot view monitor, navigation-based cruise control, parking collision-avoidance assist, parking sensors, remote smart parking assist, a surround-view monitor, highway-driving assist, and an advanced rear-occupant alert with an in-cabin radar sensor that can detect children or animals accidentally left in the vehicle — though don’t expect that last one to stick around, since Hyundai has already dropped it from 2027 models. Parking sensors are available on upper CR-V Hybrid trims. Both the CR-V Hybrid and Tucson Hybrid offer a choice between front- and all-wheel drive. On fuel economy, the CR-V Hybrid offers the most impressive figures, earning up to 43 mpg in city driving and 40 mpg combined for the front-drive model. The best the Tucson Hybrid can manage is 38 mpg combined. If saving money at the pump is your top priority, the Honda wins all day long. A two-mpg headline difference does not always translate directly to the same real-world fuel savings, so see what EPA city, highway, and combined fuel-economy ratings actually mean ➜ When it comes to price, the Hyundai Tucson Hybrid beats the Honda CR-V Hybrid. Every trim except its top level is more affordable than the least expensive CR-V Hybrid. Both models top out in the lower $40,000s, but if features matter more to you than fuel economy, the Tucson Hybrid is your best bet. Both of these vehicles are pleasant to drive, with comfortable ride quality and handling that's capable, if not sports-car-like. However, the driving experience differs quite a bit due to their different hybrid architectures. The Honda's hybrid system is configured to run mostly as a series hybrid and packs nearly three times the electric motor output of the Tucson Hybrid's. During most driving, only the electric motor drives the wheels, with the engine only turning a generator to provide electricity. A clutch engages to send some engine power to the wheels at highway speeds. The result is a quiet overall ride that feels more like driving an EV. The Hyundai's hybrid system uses a smaller motor sandwiched between the engine and a conventional six-speed automatic transmission. That makes it feel much more like a traditional gas-only vehicle, albeit generally quieter. It doesn’t have the overall refinement of the Honda, however. For more time behind the wheel of Hyundai’s turbo-hybrid setup, see how the Tucson Hybrid balances power, refinement, space, and family usability ➜ Either way, you get a surprisingly roomy crossover that delivers excellent fuel efficiency and a long feature list. The Hyundai feels a bit more modern inside, with larger screens and a bolder exterior design, while the Honda goes a bit more traditional all around. Functionality, though, is pretty similar between the two. Choosing between the CR-V Hybrid and Tucson Hybrid really comes down to personal preference. If you want a design that stands out from the crowd, the Tucson Hybrid is absolutely your winner. The front-wheel-drive CR-V Hybrid will yield you a couple of extra mpg, but those fuel savings aren’t quite enough to overcome the price gap of over $3,000 more upfront on base trims. If you want the most EV-like driving experience without a plug, get the CR-V Hybrid. title: Ream v. US Department of the Treasury Brief: Restore the Original Meaning of the Commerce Clause - Cato Institute
content: Sign up to have blog posts delivered straight to your inbox! A former aerospace engineer and current homebrewer, Ohioan John Ream wants to distill spirits at home to enjoy with his wife. He would gladly register a still and pay the relevant federal tax, but an 1868 federal law prohibits home distilling. Operating a still in your home—or on a parcel “connected with” it—is a federal felony. Ream sued the government, alleging that this ban violates the Constitution. The Sixth Circuit upheld the ban as a necessary and proper means of enforcing the federal tax on distilled spirits, thereby breaking with a Fifth Circuit decision issued just 11 days earlier. Cato filed an amicus brief urging the Supreme Court to review Ream’s case and reverse the decision. Americans distilled spirits on their homesteads well before independence. Colonial Americans enjoyed drinking rum and grain whiskey, and by 1770, New England alone had over 150 distilleries. Prominent Founders, including George Washington, operated successful distilleries on their homesteads. Yet today, the federal government has banned home distilling outright. Ream is right that this ban exceeds Congress’s constitutional powers. In James Madison’s words, “The powers delegated by the … Constitution to the federal government are few and defined.” Congress possesses only those powers enumerated in the Constitution. Yet over time, judicial expansion of the commerce clause and the necessary and proper clause has transformed a limited power to regulate interstate trade into a sweeping license to regulate nearly all human activity—and even inactivity. The result is a national police power untethered from the Constitution’s original understanding and incompatible with the liberty-preserving structure it established. The original public meaning of the commerce clause was that Congress could regulate the trade and transportation of goods and people across state lines. It did not convey authority to control or prohibit purely intrastate activity such as home distilling. Unfortunately, the Supreme Court has strayed from that original understanding. In the New Deal–era case Wickard v. Filburn, the Court held that the commerce clause authorizes Congress to regulate even a farmer’s growing and consuming wheat entirely on his own farm. The Court reasoned that Congress may regulate local activities if, in the aggregate, they exert a substantial economic effect on interstate commerce. In the 2005 decision Gonzales v. Raich, the Court extended Wickard’s reasoning further, upholding the federal prohibition on the private, intrastate cultivation and use of marijuana. The majority first concluded that the plaintiffs’ marijuana activities were “economic.” It further held that courts need not determine whether regulated activities actually substantially affect interstate commerce in the aggregate, but only whether Congress had a “rational basis” for concluding that they do. Raich is the apex of congressional authority to regulate intrastate activity. It is time to restore the Constitution’s first principle of limited national power and overturn Raich. This case presents an ideal vehicle. By extending federal criminal law to purely in-home, noncommercial activity, the decision below collapses the distinction between national and state authority and erases structural limits that preserve federalism. The Constitution does not require another century of overreach—it demands fidelity to its text and original design. The Court should grant the petition for a writ of certiorari, overrule Raich, and reaffirm that federal powers are both enumerated and limited. Every weekday morning: independent analysis grounded in individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and peace.

title: Prima Facie Is Not the End of the Analysis: Gabriel v. Top 8 Construction (via Passle) - Ropers Majeski
content: When the injured worker is the only witness to his own fall and the record holds two versions of it, based on credible evidence, he does not get summary judgment under Labor Law 240(1). The Second Department reaffirmed that last week. In Gabriel v Top 8 Constr. Corp. (2026), an electrician's helper fell from a six-foot A-frame ladder while running a cable through an open-framed ceiling. He moved for partial summary judgment before discovery closed. Kings County denied the motion, adhered on reargument, and the Second Department affirmed. The Court agreed that the plaintiff made his prima facie showing. Testimony that the ladder "suddenly shook," causing him to fall, was enough on its own. Defendants still beat it. They raised a triable issue on sole proximate cause, and where "credible evidence reveals differing versions of the accident, one under which defendants would be liable and another under which they would not, questions of fact exist, making summary judgment inappropriate." What defeated the motion is significant. The employer produced a foreman's affidavit recounting the plaintiff's own statement that he had set two ladder feet on a piece of drywall. Plaintiff's own post-accident photographs showed the drywall. A safety engineer opined that a non-defective A-frame was an adequate device for the work. This site uses cookies.
